summary:
Paid digital advertising has been tested at scale, and the results are mostly null. An eight-month, $8.9 million Facebook and Instagram programme aimed at about 2 million persuadable US voters had no net effect on turnout (D9-F01). Ads randomised by ZIP code moved vote share by -0.04 pp (SE 0.85) (D9-F02). The one test in a European multiparty election (Berlin 2016) found +0.7 pp for the sponsor, which was not significant, and most of it came from its nearest rivals (D9-F03). Ads did not raise candidate name recognition (D9-F04). They raised turnout only in low-salience, competitive races (D9-F05). Both digital and TV studies find that ads change who votes rather than how many (D9-F01, D9-F09). Ad persuasion is small and fades within days, and tested creative beats untested (P-F04 to P-F07). Targeting by one coarse attribute adds up to about 70% to persuasion; adding more attributes adds nothing (D9-F07).

Content passed along personal ties does more. In the 61-million-user Facebook experiment, the effect passed to close friends exceeded the direct effect (D9-F06). In Tamil Nadu, party WhatsApp groups moved moderate voters, mainly through posts by other members (D9-F13). People reshare debunks from close or like-minded contacts, and audio works best (D9-F14). Among Jewish Israelis, 65% get news via WhatsApp and 44% via Telegram. They trust family and friends' groups (above 60%) far more than politician-run groups (39-47%) (D9-F30). Israeli WhatsApp discussion is less polarised than discussion on X (D9-F34). For about three years Likud campaigned mainly through WhatsApp groups and a Telegram chatbot, which leave no public record, before returning to paid Meta ads in late August (D9-F28).

Partisan media matter more than ads over time. Israel Hayom added at least two seats to the right across 2009-2015, through persuasion rather than turnout (D9-F10). Channel 12 is the main news source for 51% of Jewish Israelis and draws about twice Channel 14's evening audience. Channel 14 reaches about a quarter of the right and almost no one in the centre or on the left (D9-F30, D9-F31). Debates do not move votes (P-F03). Endorsements work where party cues are weak (D9-F11), which in 2026 means choices inside the bloc and winning back voters of lists below the threshold. Negative ads are no more effective than positive ones (D9-F12).

Fact-checks correct beliefs (d of about 0.29) but not candidate support (D9-F18, D9-F19). Rebuttals from unexpected, same-side messengers work best (D9-F20). Prebunking videos raised recognition of manipulation techniques by about 5% at five US cents per view (D9-F16), but prebunking games may breed blanket scepticism (D9-F17), and media-literacy training failed in India (D9-F15). Fake news mostly reaches a small, committed minority (D9-F21). Deepfakes lower opinions of the leader they depict (D9-F22), but no 2024 election result was shown to have been changed by AI content (D9-F23). AI dialogue persuades more than ads do (D9-F08).

Israeli rules: paid TV and radio ads are banned. Allocated broadcasts run only in the final 14 days (from about 13 October). Every ad must name who ordered it, and security-forces imagery needs written consent. Since 23 July 2026, deepfakes need a full-duration label (D9-F24, D9-F25). The committee has ordered takedowns against Likud, RZP and Yashar (D9-F26). The State Comptroller found no national policy against foreign influence (D9-F29).

For the next 14 days:
(1) Move money from paid turnout ads to supporters' own WhatsApp networks, supplied with short, tested audio and video.
(2) Run paid persuasion on 21-26 October, with tested creative and one targeting attribute.
(3) Win earned reach on Channel 12 and ynet.
(4) Staff a rapid-response cell now. It should monitor the Meta Ad Library, keep committee petitions ready, use right-credentialed messengers and audio debunks, and prebunk predictable election-day stories such as station-turnout scares (D5-F27).
(5) Audit the bloc's own creative for AI labels and military imagery.

The search budget ran out before Channel 14 effects, a 2026 debate and Arabic-media surveys could be checked.

findings.topic: Paid social-media ads and turnout (largest field experiment)
findings.claim: An eight-month Facebook and Instagram persuasion campaign, aimed at about 2 million moderate and low-information persuadable voters in five US battleground states in 2020, had no net effect on turnout. Turnout rose slightly among voters modelled as Biden leaners and fell slightly among Trump leaners. The authors conclude that even very large digital ad programmes have at most modest mobilisation effects in a presidential election.
findings.quant: US$8.9M; about 2M people randomised. Overall turnout effect about 0 (reported ATE -0.06 pp). Biden leaners +0.4 pp, Trump leaners -0.3 pp; difference 0.7 pp (p = 0.036, marginal). Early-vote differences are labelled exploratory.
findings.authors: Minali Aggarwal; Jennifer Allen; Alexander Coppock; Dan Frankowski; Solomon Messing; Kelly Zhang; James Barnes; Andrew Beasley; Harry Hantman; Sylvan Zheng
findings.title: A 2 million-person, campaign-wide field experiment shows how digital advertising affects voter turnout
findings.relevance: Paid social ads are not a turnout tool for a high-salience Knesset race. Set their turnout value to about 0, which matches D3-F11. Ads aimed at soft Netanyahu-bloc voters might lower their turnout a little, but the estimate is marginal and should not be counted. Use paid digital for persuasion, rescue and recruiting volunteers, not for get-out-the-vote.

findings.topic: Paid Facebook/Instagram ads and vote share (geo-randomised)
findings.claim: A Democratic-leaning PAC's Facebook and Instagram ads in Florida's 2018 midterms were randomised by ZIP code. The ads promoted the Democratic Party and criticised the Republicans without naming candidates. The effect on Democratic vote share was essentially zero, and effects on vote margin and turnout were small and not significant.
findings.quant: Over 1 million views and over 100,000 full views. Effect on Democratic precinct vote share -0.04 pp (SE 0.85).
findings.authors: Alexander Coppock; Donald P. Green; Ethan Porter
findings.title: Does digital advertising affect vote choice? Evidence from a randomized field experiment
findings.relevance: Generic, party-brand ads for the bloc ('the change camp' against 'the Netanyahu government') should be valued at about zero for vote share. If paid digital is used, put it behind tested, list-specific and information-rich creative (P-F05, P-F11), not bloc-level image ads.

findings.topic: Online ads in a European multiparty election (Berlin 2016)
findings.claim: A German party's Facebook and Google ad campaign in the 2016 Berlin state election was randomised across 189 postal districts into emotional ads, factual ads or no ads. The party's vote share rose slightly and its main competitors' share fell, but neither estimate is significant. Factual ads did at least as well as emotional ones. Secondary accounts report no turnout effect.
findings.quant: Sponsor vote share +0.7 pp (p = 0.155). Main competitors -1.4 pp (p = 0.094). 189 postal districts.
findings.authors: Anselm Hager
findings.title: Do Online Ads Influence Vote Choice?
findings.relevance: This is the closest analogue to Israel: proportional representation, many parties, ads delivered by area. The upper bound is under 1 pp in saturated areas, and the gain came mostly from neighbouring parties. For the four change-bloc lists, paid ads will mostly move votes inside the bloc. Coordinate creative so the lists do not spend against each other in the same areas, and split ad areas the way field turf is split (MODEL_BRIEF: lead_change_list).

findings.topic: Facebook ads and name recognition / favourability
findings.claim: Two randomised Facebook ad experiments for US candidates in 2012 found that exposed voters were sometimes more likely to recall the ads. They were not more likely to recognise the candidates or to rate them favourably.
findings.quant: Survey samples of about 2,984 and 3,577 voters in the two districts (per J-PAL summary). Name recognition and favourability effects about 0.
findings.authors: David E. Broockman; Donald P. Green
findings.title: Do Online Advertisements Increase Political Candidates' Name Recognition or Favorability? Evidence from Randomized Field Experiments
findings.relevance: Low-cost ads alone are unlikely to teach new lists' identities. Examples are Yashar, and Together's ballot letters (בד) for Bennett-Lapid voters. Ballot-letter recognition should be taught through allocated broadcasts, earned media and personal contact, with paid digital only as a supplement.

findings.topic: Digital ads can mobilise only in low-salience, competitive settings
findings.claim: A preregistered field experiment with The Dallas Morning News ran information plus voting-reminder ads to millennial voters in a non-partisan May 2017 municipal election. Turnout rose only in competitive districts. The authors say the effect was comparable to live-caller phone campaigns.
findings.quant: About US$50,000 campaign. Effect under 1 pp: about 0.9% in press coverage, cited as 0.52 pp in competitive districts in later work by the first author. No effect in uncompetitive districts.
findings.authors: Katherine Haenschen; Jay Jennings
findings.title: Mobilizing Millennial Voters with Targeted Internet Advertisements: A Field Experiment
findings.relevance: A Knesset election is high-salience, so expect about 0 from reminder ads. The one sensible digital reminder is practical information for young voters registered at a parent's address: where their polling station is and that intercity transport is free (D5-F28). That message targets a real cost, not motivation.

findings.topic: Social transmission through close friends (Facebook 61-million experiment)
findings.claim: Adds to D3-F11. On US election day 2010, a Facebook message showing faces of friends who had voted raised validated turnout, and the effect also spread to recipients' friends. The indirect effect through the network was larger than the direct effect, and nearly all of it ran between close friends, who were more likely to know each other face to face.
findings.quant: 61 million users. Direct effect about +0.39 pp (D3-F11). Estimated about 60,000 votes directly and about 280,000 more through social contagion (about 340,000 in total). Indirect-to-direct ratio about 4.7.
findings.authors: Robert M. Bond; Christopher J. Fariss; Jason J. Jones; Adam D. I. Kramer; Cameron Marlow; Jaime E. Settle; James H. Fowler
findings.title: A 61-million-person experiment in social influence and political mobilization
findings.relevance: Campaigns cannot buy this feature, but they can copy the mechanism. Ask supporters to post 'I voted' and 'I'm voting for X' to their own family and friends' WhatsApp groups on 26-27 October. This complements relational organising (D3-F12). Clear election-day posting with counsel, and post nothing from inside polling stations. Do not turn it into public shaming or 'who hasn't voted' lists, which run into the backlash in D3-F05 and the 17 Sept High Court ruling (D5-F25).

findings.topic: Targeting and microtargeting returns
findings.claim: In large survey experiments with video ads on two US policy issues, targeting a message by a single attribute such as party could be up to about 70% more persuasive than showing everyone the single best message. Targeting on several attributes added nothing. The gains varied by issue and were smaller in the confirmatory experiment. Outcomes were policy support, not vote choice.
findings.quant: Phase 1 over 23,000 respondents; phase 2 over 5,000. Single-attribute targeting up to about +70% relative to the best generic ad. Multi-attribute: no further gain.
findings.authors: Ben M. Tappin; Chloe Wittenberg; Luke B. Hewitt; Adam J. Berinsky; David G. Rand
findings.title: Quantifying the potential persuasive returns to political microtargeting
findings.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 120(25) (doi:10.1073/pnas.2216261120)
findings.relevance: Build creative variants by one coarse segment that changes the argument: secular suburban, traditional (masorti), religious-Zionist, Russian-speaking, reservist families. Do not slice into many micro-audiences. With 14 days left, one round of tests per segment is feasible (P-F05).

findings.topic: Conversational (AI) persuasion vs ads
findings.claim: In randomised experiments around the 2024 US, 2025 Canadian and 2025 Polish elections, participants chatted with an AI model arguing for one of the two leading candidates. This moved candidate preferences more than benchmarks for traditional ads. Effects were much larger in Canada and Poland than in the US. They were driven by factual, policy-focused content, and part of the effect lasted a month. Participants knew they were talking to an AI advocate, so the effect in real campaigns is unknown.
findings.quant: US (about 2,300): pro-Harris model moved Trump leaners 3.9 points on a 0-100 scale; pro-Trump model moved Harris leaners 1.5. Canada (1,530) and Poland (2,118): about 10 points. About one third of the effect remained after a month (reported). Models arguing for right-wing candidates made more inaccurate claims.
findings.authors: Hause Lin; Gabriela Czarnek; Benjamin Lewis; Joshua P. White; Adam J. Berinsky; Thomas Costello; Gordon Pennycook; David G. Rand
findings.title: Persuading voters using human-artificial intelligence dialogues
findings.relevance: Two-way, evidence-rich conversation persuades more than broadcast messages, especially in multiparty systems with less familiar options. Israel's within-bloc choice and soft-right voters fit that description. Practical use: give volunteers and relational organisers fact-dense talking points. Any voter-facing chatbot would need election counsel's clearance, clear AI disclosure and a fact-checked knowledge base, and must not use realistic synthetic audio or video of people (D9-F25).

findings.topic: Broadcast ads change who votes, not how many
findings.claim: Using differences in presidential ad volumes across the borders of neighbouring US counties (2004-2012), advertising had a meaningful effect on candidates' vote shares and almost no effect on aggregate turnout. A regression-discontinuity analysis suggests the vote-share effect works by changing the partisan make-up of who turns out.
findings.quant: A one-SD increase in the partisan ad difference raises the partisan vote-share difference by about 0.5 pp. Effect on total turnout about 0, and estimates rule out even moderate effects.
findings.authors: Jorg L. Spenkuch; David Toniatti
findings.title: Political Advertising and Election Results
findings.relevance: Paid TV is banned in Israel (D9-F24), but the mechanism applies to online video and the allocated broadcasts. Mass media mainly rally one's own leaners and dampen the other side, which matches D9-F01. Value media in net-vote terms and expect small effects. Complements P-F08.

findings.topic: Partisan free newspaper and Knesset vote (Israel Hayom)
findings.claim: Israel Hayom is a free, pro-Netanyahu daily launched in 2007 that quickly became Israel's most-read paper. Using local exposure and an instrument based on readership of the rival Yedioth Ahronoth before 2007, the authors find it raised support for Likud and the right bloc in the 2009, 2013 and 2015 elections. The effect came through persuasion, not turnout, and was largest in localities split evenly between left and right.
findings.quant: At least 2 seats for the right bloc across three elections, an effect the researchers call an underestimate (as reported). 2013: each 1 pp more exposure, about +0.22 pp right-bloc vote (reported). No link between exposure and turnout.
findings.authors: Guy Grossman; Yotam Margalit; Tamar Mitts
findings.title: How the Ultrarich Use Media Ownership as a Political Investment
findings.venue: Journal of Politics 84(4): 1913-1931 (doi:10.1086/719415); effect sizes from +972 Magazine report of the working paper, 14 Sept 2020
findings.relevance: This is the best Israeli causal evidence that sustained partisan media move seats. The Netanyahu bloc's media ecosystem (Israel Hayom, Channel 14: D9-F30) is a structural persuasion asset that two weeks of change-bloc spending cannot match. Its effect was strongest in mixed localities, the same Route 4 and mid-cluster places the atlas targets. The bloc should seek earned and paid reach there through mainstream outlets read by soft-right voters, including printed newspaper ads within the legal size limits (D9-F24).

findings.topic: Celebrity endorsements
findings.claim: Using geographic variation in Oprah Winfrey's audience (magazine subscriptions and sales of her book-club titles), the authors estimate that her endorsement of Obama in the 2008 Democratic primary raised his vote, his contributions and overall turnout. A placebo test on Obama's 2004 Illinois Senate primary found no such relationship.
findings.quant: About 1 million additional Obama votes in the 2008 primary season.
findings.authors: Craig Garthwaite; Timothy J. Moore
findings.title: Can Celebrity Endorsements Affect Political Outcomes? Evidence from the 2008 US Democratic Presidential Primary
findings.venue: Journal of Law, Economics, and Organization 29(2): 355-384
findings.relevance: The evidence comes from a primary, where there is no party cue. That makes endorsements most useful for choices inside the bloc and for winning back voters of lists below the threshold. A Gantz statement if Blue and White withdraws, or reservist commanders addressing Reservists-Economic voters respectfully (MODEL_BRIEF rules), are the obvious uses. Israeli law bars entertainment and artist performances at propaganda events (s.8, D9-F24), so celebrities can appear in statements and video but not perform. Messengers must fit the audience (P-F14).

findings.topic: Negative campaigning (meta-analysis)
findings.claim: A meta-analysis of 111 studies found negative campaigning is no more effective than positive campaigning. At best it modestly lowers positive feelings toward the target. Turnout effects are mixed, and the most consistent finding is slightly lower political efficacy and trust.
findings.quant: 111 studies through mid-2006. Turnout: 57 studies with mixed signs. Knowledge rose in 11 of 15 studies.
findings.authors: Richard R. Lau; Lee Sigelman; Ivy Brown Rovner
findings.title: The Effects of Negative Political Campaigns: A Meta-Analytic Reassessment
findings.relevance: Netanyahu is fully known (P-F11), so attack ads on him gain little persuasion and can deepen affective polarisation (P-F15). Spend on information-rich contrast about the change bloc's leaders and on issues the bloc owns, such as equal burden and October 7 accountability (D5-F21). Keep attack content for rapid rebuttal.

findings.topic: Party WhatsApp groups and voter preferences (India)
findings.claim: Before the 2021 Tamil Nadu election, participants recruited on Facebook were randomly invited to join a constituency WhatsApp group of a major party, a replica group carrying only the party's own posts, or no group. Full groups raised political knowledge and moved moderate voters toward the assigned party without raising hostility to the other side. The party-only replica had smaller effects, which the author attributes to peer-to-peer posts.
findings.quant: Over 3,000 participants in 25 constituencies; 49% joined when invited. Knowledge +0.17 SD (confidence in true headlines +0.48 SD). Belief in false headlines down, not significant. Relative party rating +0.072 SD, driven by moderates. No effect on affective polarisation. Full groups had significantly larger effects than party-only groups.
findings.authors: Kevin Carney
findings.title: The Effect of Social Media on Voters: Experimental Evidence from an Indian Election (summarised as 'The WhatsApp effect: Evidence on political engagement, preferences and polarisation')
findings.venue: Working paper (also NBER conference paper, 2023); Ideas for India summary, 16 Aug 2022
findings.relevance: This is the best causal evidence on closed-group campaigning. Effects are modest, they concentrate among moderates, and they depend on conversation between members rather than broadcast. For the bloc, the format to build is supporter-led local or community WhatsApp groups with real members talking, not party broadcast channels.

findings.topic: Social debunking on WhatsApp: strong ties and audio
findings.claim: Experiments with WhatsApp users in India and Pakistan found people were more likely to reshare a debunking message when it came from someone close to them, from someone who shared their politics, or both. Debunks delivered as audio files drew more interest and corrected beliefs better than text or image versions.
findings.authors: Irene V. Pasquetto; Eaman Jahani; Shubham Atreja; Matthew Baum
findings.title: Social Debunking of Misinformation on WhatsApp: The Case for Strong and In-group Ties
findings.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction 6(CSCW1), Article 117 (doi:10.1145/3512964)
findings.relevance: Rapid-response packages should be short voice notes and vertical videos sent to supporters so they forward them to their own family and community groups, not posted only on official pages. This fits Israeli trust patterns: family and friends' groups are trusted more than politician-run groups (D9-F30).

findings.topic: Media-literacy training in a polarised election (India)
findings.claim: During India's 2019 election, an hour-long in-person training in verification and inoculation, with corrections of false stories, did not improve people's ability to identify misinformation two weeks later. Trained supporters of the ruling party became worse at spotting false stories that favoured their own side.
findings.quant: N = 1,224 (Bihar). Average effect not significantly different from 0. Backfire among ruling-party supporters on pro-attitudinal items.
findings.authors: Sumitra Badrinathan
findings.title: Educative Interventions to Combat Misinformation: Evidence from a Field Experiment in India
findings.relevance: Do not spend the last two weeks on generic 'think before you share' campaigns. Israeli blocs are affectively polarised (D1-F04), and motivated reasoning will blunt them. Concentrate on specific prebunks and on rebuttals delivered by trusted messengers (D9-F14, D9-F16, D9-F20).

findings.topic: Prebunking / inoculation videos at scale
findings.claim: Short videos that explain manipulation techniques (emotional language, false dichotomies, scapegoating, ad hominem, incoherence) improved people's ability to recognise those techniques in six lab experiments. In a YouTube field test run as pre-roll ads, recognition rose by about 5% on average about 18 hours after viewing, just below the preregistered smallest effect of interest.
findings.quant: Lab: 6 experiments, n = 6,464. Field: ads shown to about 5.4M US users, about 1M watched at least 30 s, and 22,632 answered a test item within 24 h (mean about 18 h). Recognition +5% on average. Cost about US$0.05 per meaningful view.
findings.authors: Jon Roozenbeek; Sander van der Linden; Beth Goldberg; Steve Rathje; Stephan Lewandowsky
findings.title: Psychological inoculation improves resilience against misinformation on social media
findings.relevance: This is cheap enough to run as pre-roll in the final week, aimed at the bloc's own and soft voters. Prebunk the specific manipulations likely in the last days: AI fakes linking change-bloc leaders to Arab or PA leaders (D9-F26), and 'look who is flocking to the polls' turnout scares built on the committee's station turnout releases (D5-F26, D5-F27). Effects were measured within a day, so time prebunks close to the expected attack.

findings.topic: Caveat: inoculation games raise scepticism, not discernment
findings.claim: A reanalysis of five studies of the Bad News and Go Viral! games used signal-detection (ROC) methods. The games did not improve the ability to tell true from false news. They made players more likely to rate all news, true or false, as false.
findings.quant: Discrimination unchanged; conservative response bias increased. Replications report the same pattern for Bad News.
findings.authors: Ariana Modirrousta-Galian; Philip A. Higham
findings.title: Gamified inoculation interventions do not improve discrimination between true and fake news: Reanalyzing existing research with receiver operating characteristic analysis
findings.relevance: Generic 'everything online is fake' messages can also discount the bloc's true content, including real recordings and accountability material on October 7. Prebunk named, specific claims or techniques, and pair them with verifiable evidence the bloc wants believed.

findings.topic: Fact-checking effects (meta-analysis)
findings.claim: Across 30 studies, fact-checks improved the accuracy of political beliefs. Effects were weaker when fact-checks used graded 'truth scales', refuted only part of a claim, or addressed campaign statements. Prior beliefs, ideology and knowledge also weakened them substantially.
findings.quant: k = 30, N = 20,963. Overall d = 0.29. Weakest for campaign-related claims.
findings.authors: Nathan Walter; Jonathan Cohen; R. Lance Holbert; Yasmin Morag
findings.title: Fact-Checking: A Meta-Analysis of What Works and for Whom
findings.relevance: Rebuttals should be complete and flat ('this meeting never happened; here is the committee ruling'), not 'mostly false' ratings. Expect small effects on contested campaign claims. Rapid response defends the bloc's own voters and soft voters more than it converts opponents.

findings.topic: Fact-checks fix beliefs but not candidate support
findings.claim: Two experiments during the 2016 US campaign tested realistic fact-checks of Donald Trump's claims from his convention speech and a debate. The fact-checks made factual beliefs more accurate, including among Trump supporters, but had no measurable effect on attitudes toward Trump.
findings.quant: Belief accuracy improved significantly. Candidate favourability effect about 0.
findings.authors: Brendan Nyhan; Ethan Porter; Jason Reifler; Thomas J. Wood
findings.title: Taking Fact-Checks Literally But Not Seriously? The Effects of Journalistic Fact-Checking on Factual Beliefs and Candidate Favorability
findings.relevance: Fact-checking Netanyahu-bloc claims will not move bloc-committed voters' votes. Rapid response should aim to stop false claims spreading into soft-voter networks and to keep the bloc's own coalition from being demoralised. It should not be judged by whether it converts opponents.

findings.topic: Rebuttal messenger: unlikely sources work best; repetition helps rumours
findings.claim: Experiments on the US 'death panels' rumour found that simply repeating a rumour makes it more believable, and that corrections from an unexpected partisan source (a Republican) worked better than nonpartisan or Democratic corrections. The advantage was short-lived.
findings.quant: Rumour rejection: about 58% with a Republican-source correction, about 51% with a nonpartisan correction, about 53% with a Democratic correction (as reported in secondary summaries). First experiment n = 1,701.
findings.authors: Adam J. Berinsky
findings.title: Rumors and Health Care Reform: Experiments in Political Misinformation
findings.relevance: Attacks aimed at soft-right voters, such as 'Eisenkot will sit with the Arab parties', should be answered by right-credentialed messengers: Bennett, Liberman, Eisenkot and religious-Zionist or reservist figures, not left-coded ones (P-F14). Do not repeat the false claim in headlines. Lead with the true statement.

findings.topic: Misinformation exposure is highly concentrated
findings.claim: Matching Twitter accounts to US voter records in 2016 showed that fake-news sources made up about 6% of political news consumption. Exposure and sharing were extremely concentrated in a small, mostly strongly partisan group.
findings.quant: 1% of users saw 80% of fake-news exposures; 0.1% shared 80% of fake news.
findings.authors: Nir Grinberg; Kenneth Joseph; Lisa Friedland; Briony Swire-Thompson; David Lazer
findings.title: Fake news on Twitter during the 2016 U.S. presidential election
findings.relevance: Triage. Most false content reaches people already committed to the other bloc. The rapid-response cell should act when a claim moves into mainstream outlets (Channel 12/13, ynet) or into soft-voter and Russian-speaking networks, and should ignore content that circulates only among committed partisans.

findings.topic: Deepfake effects on attitudes
findings.claim: In an online experiment in the Netherlands, a video-and-audio deepfake of a Christian Democrat (CDA) politician lowered attitudes toward the politician but not toward his party overall. In the subgroup the fake was tailored to, attitudes toward both the politician and the party fell.
findings.quant: N = 278. Politician evaluation significantly lower (p = .01), concentrated among non-CDA voters. Party evaluation unchanged overall and lower in the targeted subgroup.
findings.authors: Tom Dobber; Nadia Metoui; Damian Trilling; Natali Helberger; Claes de Vreese
findings.title: Do (Microtargeted) Deepfakes Have Real Effects on Political Attitudes?
findings.relevance: Lists built around one leader (Yashar/Eisenkot, Together/Bennett, YB/Liberman) are exposed to leader-targeted fakes, especially fakes tailored to soft-right or traditional audiences. Prepare authenticated source footage, a committee petition template and a trusted-messenger rebuttal in advance (D9-F25, D9-F26).

findings.topic: AI-generated content and 2024 election outcomes
findings.claim: The Alan Turing Institute's Centre for Emerging Technology and Security (CETaS) found no conclusive evidence that AI-generated mis- or disinformation meaningfully changed any 2024 election result. It points to the small volume of such content and to its audiences being already aligned with it. It warns of indirect harms: confusion about what is real, lower trust in online sources, and hate directed at candidates.
findings.quant: A CETaS review of 112 national elections (since January 2023 or scheduled for 2024) found examples of AI-enabled interference in 19.
findings.authors: Centre for Emerging Technology and Security (CETaS), The Alan Turing Institute (Sam Stockwell et al.)
findings.title: AI-Enabled Influence Operations: Safeguarding Future Elections (and related CETaS briefings); summarised in written evidence RGE 11 to the UK Parliament
findings.venue: CETaS research report / UK Parliament written evidence
findings.relevance: Do not over-invest in deepfake panic. The realistic damage is to trust and leader image at the margin (D9-F22), and the 'liar's dividend' (dismissing real material as fake). Respond quickly and in proportion. Keep the bloc's own AI use clean so the bloc can credibly call out others (D9-F25).

findings.topic: Israeli law: broadcasts, ad identification, soldiers' images, entertainment, polls
findings.claim: The Elections (Propaganda Methods) Law bans election propaganda on radio and TV in the 60 days before the election, except allocated election broadcasts. Those broadcasts may run only in the 14 days before the election, with no TV broadcasts on fixed rest days. Each list gets 7 TV minutes plus 2 per outgoing MK of the submitting faction, and 15 radio minutes plus 4 per MK. Since 2022 every election ad must carry the name and contact details of whoever ordered it, which covers paid content. A security-forces member's name or likeness may not be used without written consent, and the IDF may not be shown as affiliated with a list. Propaganda may not be combined with entertainment or artist performances, gifts, or food and alcohol except at private house meetings. Printed public ads are limited to designated boards, and newspaper ads are capped in size and volume. Poll publication must include methodological details, including online, and is banned from the end of the Friday before election day.
findings.quant: Broadcast window = final 14 days, roughly 13-26 Oct 2026 excluding Saturdays (derived from the statute; the committee's schedule was not verified). TV: 7 min per list + 2 min per outgoing MK. Radio: 15 min + 4 min per MK. Penalty for violations: up to 6 months' imprisonment or a fine (s.17).
findings.authors: Knesset (statute); text as consolidated on Hebrew Wikisource
findings.title: Elections (Propaganda Methods) Law, 5719-1959 (חוק הבחירות (דרכי תעמולה), התשי"ט-1959), ss. 2A1, 2A2, 2B, 5, 8, 10, 15, 15A, 16E, 17
findings.relevance: Broadcast airtime is fixed by law, not bought. The bloc's levers are content quality and order, not volume, and allocated slots started around today (D-14). All paid digital content needs an 'ordered by' line. Reservist and soldier imagery needs individual written consent and no IDF framing; the committee applied this even to AI-generated soldiers (D9-F26). No concerts or performers at rallies. From the end of Fri 23 Oct no poll figures (MODEL_BRIEF rules). Confirm the 2026 slot schedule and minutes with the committee and election counsel.

findings.topic: AI deepfake disclosure rule (2026)
findings.claim: A temporary provision (s.2A2) in force from 23 July 2026 to 26 October 2027 requires anyone who publishes election propaganda that is a deepfake to attach a clear and prominent disclosure. A deepfake here means visual or audio content depicting a person, place, event, document or object that was created or substantially altered by digital means, including AI, and could appear authentic. The committee's rules of 26 July 2026 set the format. Attaching a compliant notice creates a presumption of compliance.
findings.quant: Video: label for the full duration, font at least 5% of screen height or width. Audio-only: read at the start and end at normal volume and speed. Print and images: at least 5% of content height or 10 pt. Text or standard symbol (one for created, one for altered content).
findings.authors: Central Elections Committee for the 26th Knesset (chair: Justice Noam Sohlberg); summary by Pearl Cohen Zedek Latzer Baratz
findings.title: Israel Issues Deepfake Disclosure Rules for Election Campaign Publications
findings.venue: Pearl Cohen client alert (30 Jul 2026), describing CEC rules under s.2A2(b) of the Elections (Propaganda Methods) Law
findings.relevance: Every synthetic or materially altered asset the bloc publishes, including voice-cloned audio and AI video, needs the full-duration label. A label does not cure content that is misleading (see the Smotrich ruling, D9-F26). Rapid response can use the rule against opponents: an unlabelled or misleading fake is grounds for a petition. Whether the rule reaches individuals forwarding content on WhatsApp is untested (open question).

findings.topic: Committee rulings on AI and manipulated propaganda (2026)
findings.claim: In February 2026 the committee ordered Likud to remove a manipulated image showing Bennett and Lapid joining hands with Arab party leaders. On 26 July the chair ordered Smotrich and RZP to delete an AI video showing a figure resembling Eisenkot shaking hands with Mahmoud Abbas and Mansour Abbas. He held that it unfairly interfered with propaganda and that its AI caption was insufficient because Facebook users are unlikely to notice it. On 6 August the committee ordered Eisenkot to take down a video with AI-generated IDF soldiers, holding that uniforms are public property and that linking him to the IDF is prohibited. Netanyahu later shared an AI ad about Eisenkot that critics said mocked his late son; no committee action was reported.
findings.quant: Legal costs: NIS 8,500 to Bennett's party in the February case (reported in one secondary source; unverified).
findings.authors: Times of Israel liveblog; Israel National News
findings.title: Elections panel orders Eisenkot to take down AI campaign video showing IDF soldiers (6 Aug 2026); Precedential ruling against AI election ads (26 Jul 2026)
findings.venue: Times of Israel; Israel National News (Arutz Sheva)
findings.relevance: The predictable attack line is AI imagery tying change-bloc leaders to Arab or PA leaders, aimed at soft-right voters. The committee has acted on it twice, so petitions work, though only after the content has spread. The bloc's own creative is under scrutiny too: Yashar has already lost a video over military imagery. Pre-clear all military-adjacent creative with counsel.

findings.topic: Online ad transparency in Israel (platforms)
findings.claim: Before the April 2019 election, the committee chair (Justice Hanan Melcer) banned anonymous election ads on all online platforms from 1 March 2019. Facebook then required identity verification for Israeli political and election ads, added 'paid for by' disclaimers, and keeps them in a public Ad Library for seven years. Google has also run an Israel election-ads verification policy since 2020. The identification duty is now in statute (s.2A1, 2022).
findings.quant: Meta Ad Library entries show spend ranges, impressions, and the age, gender and region of the audience reached for each ad.
findings.authors: Times of Israel staff
findings.title: Facebook rolls out political ad transparency less than a month before polls
findings.relevance: Everything the bloc buys on Meta and Google is visible to Likud and to journalists, including its targeting. Assume opposition research on it and avoid targeting that could be framed as divisive. The bloc can monitor rival spending daily in the same way. WhatsApp and Telegram leave no such record (D9-F28).

findings.topic: Likud's closed-network strategy and the 2026 online ad race
findings.claim: A Haaretz analysis of Meta ad data found that Netanyahu's opponents have outspent him online for years. For nearly three years Likud largely avoided Meta ads and ran its campaign through WhatsApp groups and a Telegram chatbot, which leave no public record. About two weeks before 12 September 2026 Netanyahu resumed paid Facebook advertising and quickly outspent almost all rivals. Right-wing parties' ads mainly target men.
findings.quant: Spending figures are behind a paywall and were not retrieved.
findings.authors: Omer Benjakob
findings.title: The Money Race: How Much Israeli Politicians Are Spending on Online Ads
findings.relevance: The Netanyahu bloc's core reach runs through closed networks that the bloc cannot see, along with its partisan media (D9-F10). Outspending Likud on Meta is not an advantage given the null ad effects (D9-F01 to D9-F03). The bloc's answer is its own supporter-run networks (D9-F13, D9-F06). Pull current spend from the Meta Ad Library.

findings.topic: Bots, fake accounts and foreign influence (State Comptroller)
findings.claim: The State Comptroller's July 2026 special report found that, about nine years after the threat was identified (2017), Israel has no interagency national policy on foreign digital influence. The state's picture of the threat is incomplete, there is no data on how platforms respond to takedown requests, and the public has no formal channel for reporting. Iran and Hezbollah sent about 5 million SMS in September 2024, including a false shelter alert. The report calls on the committee to close its preparedness gap and consider a channel for receiving inquiries before the 2026 election. An earlier Comptroller report on the 2019 elections found indications that parties paid to inflate followers and ran fake accounts, but could not identify which parties. The Shin Bet chief has reportedly named Iran as the main foreign actor in 2026.
findings.quant: About 5M hostile SMS (Sept 2024). 58% of Israelis update their news often through social media (survey cited in the report). Audit period Jul 2024 - Jan 2026, status as of Mar 2026.
findings.authors: State Comptroller of Israel (Matanyahu Englman)
findings.title: ההתמודדות הלאומית עם השפעה זרה במרחב הדיגיטלי (The National Response to Foreign Influence in the Digital Space), special report
findings.venue: Office of the State Comptroller, July 2026 (Tammuz 5786); 2019-elections finding reported by Times of Israel, 30 Nov 2021
findings.relevance: The bloc cannot count on the state to detect and remove inauthentic campaigns in the final days. It needs its own monitoring: a vendor or volunteers tracking Hebrew, Russian and Arabic networks, and referrals to the committee, platforms and the police. Foreign operations reportedly target both camps and election-day trust, so prepare a 'trust the count' message for 27-28 October. Never use paid follower or fake-account tactics: the Comptroller has already flagged them, and exposure would be costly.

findings.topic: Israeli news consumption and trust by camp (Jewish public)
findings.claim: Among Jewish Israelis, Channel 12 is by far the main TV news source and Channel 14 is second, with an audience almost entirely on the right. Online sites are the most common way people get news. WhatsApp and Telegram are major news channels, and family and friends' groups are trusted more than groups run by politicians or journalists. Kan is the most trusted outlet and Channel 14 the least, but Channel 14's own viewers trust it very highly.
findings.quant: Main news source: Ch12 51%, Ch14 20%, Ch13 13%, Kan 11 13% (Ch12 primary or secondary 72.5%). Channel 14 watched by 24% of the right, 4% of the centre, 3.5% of the left. Main online source: ynet 40%, N12 24%. News via WhatsApp 65%, Telegram 44% (average 15 WhatsApp groups, 10 Telegram channels). Trust: family, friends and work groups above 60%; politician- or journalist-run groups WhatsApp 39%, Telegram 47%. Outlet trust: Kan 60%, Ch12 54%, Ch13 46%, Ch14 35%; 85% of Ch14 viewers trust it. 51% of Ch14 viewers do not watch news on Shabbat.
findings.authors: Tehilla Shwartz Altshuler; Inna Orly Sapozhnikova (Israel Democracy Institute)
findings.title: Media and Social Media Consumption, Trust, and Literacy
findings.venue: Israel Democracy Institute (26 May 2024); Jewish sample only
findings.relevance: Media mix: soft-right and traditional voters are mostly reached through Channel 12/N12 and ynet, not Channel 14. Earned-media effort should concentrate on Channel 12 and ynet news cycles. Relational WhatsApp is the most trusted channel, so it is the priority vehicle for rapid response. Politician-run broadcast groups are trusted least. An IDI 2025 survey found the same trust ordering (Kan highest, Ch14 lowest) and a wide left-right gap.

findings.topic: TV news audiences, April 2026
findings.claim: On Thursday 9 April 2026, Channel 12's evening news drew about twice Channel 14's audience and nearly three times Channel 13's. Kan 11 figures were not reported in the source.
findings.authors: ice.co.il TV ratings desk
findings.title: Evening news ratings, Thursday 9 April 2026
findings.relevance: Earned media on Channel 12 reaches roughly 400,000 households a night, a reach paid digital cannot match in trust. Leader interviews and news-making events should be timed for Channel 12 and 13 evening cycles in the final week. Channel 14 has a sizeable but closed audience (D9-F30). Ratings cover a single date; check October figures.

findings.topic: Platform use by age and sector (incl. Arab society)
findings.claim: Almost all Israeli adults use WhatsApp and YouTube, and Facebook remains near-universal among people over 30. Telegram use jumped between 2023 and 2024, and Instagram and TikTok dominate among 18-22-year-olds. Arab citizens use TikTok and Facebook more than the general population, and Telegram about as much.
findings.quant: Jan 2024 (n = 1,004 adults, Geocartography): WhatsApp 98% (95% of users daily), YouTube 98%, Facebook 87%, Instagram 75%, Telegram 70% (54% in Jan 2023), TikTok 54%, X 37%. Ages 18-22: Instagram 90%, TikTok 80%, Telegram 77%. Arab adults: TikTok 71% (58% daily). 2025 index (reported by JPost, 26 Oct 2025): Arab adults Facebook 93% (72% daily), TikTok 71% (61% daily), Telegram 71%.
findings.authors: Asaf Wiener; Ofir Stegman (Israel Internet Association, ISOC-IL)
findings.title: Social Media and Digital Platform Use in Israel (2024)
findings.venue: Israel Internet Association (21 Apr 2024); 2025 update reported in The Jerusalem Post
findings.relevance: Channel by segment: first-time and student voters through Instagram and TikTok; over-40 suburban and traditional voters through Facebook and WhatsApp. Arabic-language outreach by the lists that campaign there (the Democrats, D5-F32) runs mainly on Facebook and TikTok. Any Arab-sector turnout work is a leadership decision, independent, transparent and cleared by counsel (MODEL_BRIEF rules).

findings.topic: Russian-speaking Israelis' media
findings.claim: In a large self-selected reader poll of the Russian-language site NEWSru.co.il (January 2024), news sites dominated. Channel 9 (Russian-language Israeli TV) was the most-watched TV channel. Use of Russian-language Telegram channels for war news rose sharply after October 7. Facebook and Telegram were the main social platforms, and WhatsApp and Telegram the main messengers for news.
findings.quant: n = 2,981 (self-selected). Regular news sources: sites 87%, social networks 47%, TV 29%. TV: Channel 9 38% (29% before the war), Ch12 25%, Ch13 14%, Kan 11 12%, Ch14 12%, no TV 37%. Social: Facebook 61%, Telegram 47%, Instagram 20%, TikTok 11%. Messengers for news: WhatsApp 54%, Telegram 48%. Russian-language Telegram channels for war news 40% (18% in summer 2023).
findings.authors: NEWSru.co.il
findings.title: СМИ и соцсети в жизни русскоязычных израильтян во время войны. Итоги опроса (Media and social networks of Russian-speaking Israelis during the war: poll results)
findings.relevance: Yisrael Beytenu's Russian-speaker effort (D5-F12), and any other list's Russian-language outreach, should run on Russian-language news sites, Channel 9, Facebook and Russian-language Telegram channels. The sample is older and self-selected, so use it to choose channels, not to size reach. Russian-language Telegram is also a likely route for misinformation and needs monitoring (D9-F29).

findings.topic: Polarisation differs by platform in Israel (WhatsApp vs Twitter)
findings.claim: An analysis of about a quarter-million online contributions on Facebook, Twitter and WhatsApp about one Israeli political controversy over 16 months found that polarisation is not uniform across platforms. Twitter showed homophilic interaction, growing positional polarisation and pronounced hostility. WhatsApp discussion became less polarised over time.
findings.quant: About 250,000 contributions over 16 months on three platforms.
findings.authors: Moran Yarchi; Christian Baden; Neta Kligler-Vilenchik
findings.title: Political Polarization on the Digital Sphere: A Cross-platform, Over-time Analysis of Interactional, Positional, and Affective Polarization on Social Media
findings.relevance: X is a venue for elites and journalists, not for persuasion. Cross-pressured soft-right voters are more reachable in the less hostile settings of WhatsApp groups with people they know (D9-F13, D9-F14). Keep X for rapid-response signalling to journalists.

findings.topic: Operational risk: WhatsApp account blocking and bulk messaging
findings.claim: An IDI position paper (6 Oct 2026) warns that WhatsApp is a central tool for running election activity in Israel. A single wrongful account block can disrupt a whole operation, so it calls for early preparation and a fast-track review mechanism. WhatsApp has told parties elsewhere that it is not a channel for messaging at scale and that it bans accounts showing automated or bulk behaviour (reported for India 2019; Brazil's electoral court adopted a ban on mass political messaging).
findings.authors: Rachel Aridor Hershkowitz; Tehilla Shwartz Altshuler (with Ori Grodzinsky), Israel Democracy Institute
findings.title: חסימות שגויות של חשבונות וואטסאפ בתקופת בחירות: השלכות פוטנציאליות ונחיצותם של היערכות מוקדמת ומנגנון בחינה מזורז (Wrongful blocking of WhatsApp accounts during elections)
findings.venue: Israel Democracy Institute position paper (6 Oct 2026)
findings.relevance: Do not run relational or rescue programmes through a few coordinator accounts blasting lists. Spread sending across many real volunteer accounts with personal messages, keep backup accounts and contact exports, and avoid automation in the final 72 hours. A block on election eve is a real operational risk.

parameters.range: -0.1 to 0.3 (upper end only for practical reminders to young or low-information voters)
parameters.basis: D9-F01 (overall about 0 at 2M people), D9-F02 (turnout n.s.), D9-F05 (gains only in low-salience competitive races), D3-F11 (purchased Facebook ads 0)

parameters.basis: Assumption. D9-F03 (gain mostly from nearest competitors: -1.4 vs +0.7), P-F17 (volatility mainly within bloc), D5-F18 (within-bloc battles)

parameters.name: ad_composition_effect (turnout change among sponsor's vs opponent's leaners)
parameters.value: +0.4 pp own leaners / -0.3 pp opponent leaners
parameters.range: 0 to +/-0.5 pp; do not count in the plan
parameters.basis: D9-F01 (marginal, p = 0.036), D9-F09 (TV ads shift electorate composition, not total turnout)

parameters.name: peer_network_multiplier_on_direct_digital_effect (content shared by close ties)
parameters.basis: D9-F06 (indirect effect about 4.7x the direct, via close friends), D9-F13 (peer posts beat party-only content), D3-F12 (friend-to-friend texting)

parameters.basis: D9-F07 (up to about +70%, smaller in the confirmatory study; policy-attitude outcomes)

parameters.name: share_of_paid_persuasion_budget_in_final_six_days (21-26 Oct)
parameters.basis: P-F06, P-F07 (half-life about 3 days); D9-F16 (prebunk effects measured within about 18 h); D9-F24 (allocated broadcasts are fixed, so paid digital is the only flexible lever)

parameters.name: fact_check_belief_correction_effect_d
parameters.range: 0.1 to 0.6 (weakest for campaign claims and graded ratings)

parameters.name: prebunk_video_effect_and_cost
parameters.value: +5% technique recognition; about US$0.05 per meaningful view

parameters.name: misinformation_exposure_concentration
parameters.basis: D9-F21; respond only when a claim reaches mainstream or soft-voter networks

parameters.value: +0.22 pp right-bloc vote per +1 pp locality exposure (2013); at least 2 seats over 3 elections

parameters.name: allocated_broadcast_window_and_minutes
parameters.value: Final 14 days (about 13-26 Oct, no Saturday broadcasts); TV 7 min per list + 2 per outgoing MK; radio 15 + 4

parameters.name: news_via_messaging_apps (Jewish adults)
parameters.range: trust: family and friends' groups above 60%; politician-run groups 39-47%

parameters.name: ai_dialogue_persuasion_points (0-100 preference scale)
parameters.range: about one third persists at 1 month; lab-like setting
parameters.basis: D9-F08; not an election-day vote effect

open_questions: The committee's 2026 broadcast schedule and each change-bloc list's allocated minutes, which depend on the outgoing MKs of the submitting factions, were not verified. Get the schedule from the committee and plan slot order and content now.

How fast does the committee chair rule on deepfake and anonymous-propaganda petitions in the final week and on election day? Do its takedown orders reach content forwarded by individuals on WhatsApp and Telegram (s.2A2 applies to 'a person who publishes')?

Current Meta and Google spend by party since late August 2026 (the Haaretz figures are paywalled). Pull them directly from the Meta Ad Library and Google transparency report, and check each platform's last-day ad cut-off for Israel.

No causal study of Channel 14's electoral effect was found. The shared search budget ran out before a targeted search, so the Israel Hayom estimate (D9-F10) is the only Israeli partisan-media benchmark.
Is any 2026 leaders' TV debate scheduled? Not checked (search budget ran out). Evidence says debates do not move votes (P-F03), so value is about 0 either way.

There is no recent representative survey of Arabic-language news consumption among Arab citizens (IDI promised a companion survey to its 2024 Jewish study; not found). Platform-use data only (D9-F32).

No Israeli randomised test of digital ads, WhatsApp messaging or prebunking was found. A cheap geo-randomised test of the final-week persuasion flight would give the bloc its own estimate for future cycles.

How large is the reach of Likud's Telegram chatbot and WhatsApp group network (D9-F28), and what content does it push in the final 72 hours? This needs monitoring by volunteers who are legitimately members of public groups, without infiltration or deception.
Does the AI-disclosure rule cover synthetic voice notes recorded in a real person's voice with consent, and AI-edited real footage? Get counsel's view before using any such asset.

Will foreign influence operations attempt election-day 'results are rigged' or false-alert SMS campaigns (precedent: about 5M hostile SMS in Sept 2024, D9-F29)? Is there a committee or INCD channel for rapid reporting?
How Russian-speaking and traditional voters respond to AI-generated fakes in Russian or Hebrew; no Israeli experimental evidence found.
